articles.title: Chinese tech giants Huawei and Xiaomi launch new foldable smartphones ahead of Apple event
articles.summary: Chinese tech companies Huawei and Xiaomi launched new flagship foldable smartphones on Monday, stepping up competition in China’s premium handset market ahead of Apple’s product launch later this week.
articles.body: Chinese tech companies Huawei and Xiaomi launched new flagship foldable smartphones on Monday, stepping up competition in China’s premium handset market ahead of Apple’s product launch later this week. Huawei’s new Mate XT2 series, which fold out twice into a tablet-sized screen, features its Kirin 9050 Pro chip, a redesigned hinge, improved water resistance and a privacy screen that prevents nearby people from viewing the display. The devices are priced from 19,999 yuan ($2,980), with the top-end version costing 24,999 yuan ($3,725). Sales begin Saturday. “Pricing right now is a real challenge, because memory costs have risen sharply. We adopted a lot of new technology, and the cost pressure has been enormous,” Huawei Executive Director Richard Yu told a news conference. Huawei said the new chip design delivers greater computing power while using less electricity. The architecture, called LogicFolding, is part of the “Tau Scaling Law” principle unveiled in May as Huawei seeks to overcome U.S. restrictions on access to advanced technology. At a separate launch event, Xiaomi unveiled its most premium phone to date, the Xiaomi 18 Fold. The device uses what Xiaomi calls a “medium-fold solution,” remaining passport-sized when closed while supporting three apps side by side when opened. Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun said the device had several advantages over Apple products. Weighing less than 8 ounces and measuring less than a quarter-inch thick when unfolded, the phone is lighter than Apple’s iPhone Pro Max, he said. The handset runs Xiaomi’s in-house XRing O3 AI processor, which Lei said outperforms Apple’s A19 Pro in responsiveness. It also uses DRAM memory chips supplied by Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT. The Xiaomi 18 Fold is priced from 10,999 yuan ($1,540) to 14,999 yuan ($2,100). “Nowadays, memory is very, very expensive. We don’t say it is cheap, but it is value for money,” Lei said. The launches come ahead of Apple’s unveiling of its latest iPhone series on Wednesday, with expectations high that it could also introduce a foldable phone. Huawei is currently the only major brand selling a so-called tri-fold phone. The Chinese tech giant is barred from selling products in the U.S., where Washington has deemed it a national security risk. South Korea’s Samsung Electronics, the world’s biggest foldable smartphone vendor, launched a tri-fold device in December but reportedly discontinued sales after three months. In July, it expanded its foldable lineup to include a passport-sized foldable phone. Huawei led China’s smartphone market with a 22.6% share in the second quarter, ahead of Apple’s 18.1%, according to the consulting firm IDC. Xiaomi held a 12.4% share. Huawei was even more dominant in folding phones, accounting for 68% of shipments in China in the second quarter, according to U.S.-based research company Smart Analytics Global.

images.caption: An audience member takes a selfie with Huawei's Mate XT 2 tri-fold smartphone powered by the new Kirin 9050 Pro chip after a launch event in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Sept. 7, 2026. Chinese tech giant Huawei on Monday launched the Mate XT 2 tri-fold smartphone powered by the new Kirin 9050 Pro chip, the first high-performance processor to use logic folding technology.  The Kirin 9050 Pro stacks logic units in layers within a single chip, shortening signal transmission paths, reducing latency and boosting overall performance, according to a launch event in Guangzhou.  The last time Huawei introduced a new Kirin chip at a flagship launch was at the global release of the Mate 40 smartphone six years ago. The company has continued to innovate and break new ground in recent years. (Photo by Mao Siqian/Xinhua via Getty Images)

articles.title: 'JLR job cuts a cause for uncertainty and worry'
articles.summary: Experts say they worry it could limit the company's ability to innovate in the future.
articles.body:
News that Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) was to cut 4,000 jobs was a cause for uncertainty and stress for company workers and those in the wider supply chain, experts have said.

Prof David Bailey from the Birmingham Business School said he worried it could limit the company's ability to innovate in the future while David Roberts, chairman of Coventry-based Evtec Group, said up to 200,000 jobs could be tied to JLR.

The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office in Whitley, Coventry.

But there are concerns about the impact the job cuts will have on the West Midlands' skill base.

Why the 'Temu Range Rover' is such a threat to Jaguar Land Rover

Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years

Jaguar Land Rover boss to meet minister as thousands of job cuts expected

"The danger there is, in part, if they cut for example too many workers in research and development that could affect their future ability to develop new cars," Bailey said.

"So it's a really critical phase for the company and there's going to be real concern at the firm about what's happening."

He said he understood JLR was facing a range of issues, but cutting the workforce was risky.

"When margins are squeezed, companies cut costs and investment; when investment is delayed, the UK becomes less competitive; and when competitiveness falls, future investment increasingly goes elsewhere," he said.

Bailey said the British motor industry needed government help to compete in the electric car market and it was crucial to more than jobs on the factory floor.

He said: "It anchors research and development, engineering capability, component suppliers and regional economies.

"Once those capabilities disappear, they are extremely difficult to recreate."

Evtec supplies parts to JLR and chairman David Roberts said it was a "worrying time".

"A lot of the jobs here, if they go, they go, they leave the sector," he said.

"And these are jobs with real skills that take years to build and it's easier to lose them."

JLR has been dealing with falling sales, the consequences of a devastating cyber-attack that paralysed production last year, competition from China and rising energy prices.

At the same time, it has invested billions in an effort to reinvent itself for an electric future.

Dr Steve McCabe, a political economist from Birmingham City University, said he believed the job cuts were a strategic move.

"What JLR are trying to do is clean themselves up and make themselves more efficient in the hope that alowes them to survive," he said.

"The hope is of course that its a temporary thing," he added.

The company's reinvention is due to take another step forward when it unveils a new electric car on 6 October.

Kevin Moreley, a former managing director of the Rover Group believes it could be a pivotal moment.

He said: "I always thought that only 300 redundancies for JLR was a little optimistic given the new Jaguar launch is still unpredictable, and VW are making 100,000 workers redundant.

"4,000 will not be the end of it if the new Jaguar doesn't sell the numbers they hope."

There are concerns about the impact the job cuts will have on the region's skill base.

Emily Stubbs, head of policy at Greater Birmingham Chambers of Commerce, said: "We've got deep advanced manufacturing skills base here in the West Midlands.

"The government, employers, training providers, need to work together to retain that within the regional economy."

Richard Parker, Mayor of the West Midlands, said: "These are highly skilled people and I want those skills to stay here in the West Midlands."

The Combined Authority had put together a £500,000 support package for JLR workers who take voluntary redundancy, he said.

He said more support may become available in the future and described JLR as "hugely important to our region".

articles.title: Studland seahorse survey success but storms threaten habitat
articles.summary: With increasing winter storms predicted vital habitat for seahorses could be under threat
articles.body:
The increasing chances of more severe storms could put the South's seagrass meadows at risk.

Work to recover the precious habitat at sites such as Studland Bay in Dorset has seen encouraging signs of species, including seahorses, returning.

But potential damage to the seagrass due to shifting weather patterns could put that recovery under threat.

While the unique marine flowering plant can help reduce the erosion of the seabed in shallow water it is vulnerable to stormy weather.

For the team of volunteers who survey Studland Bay it has been a busy summer.

Last year saw the highest recorded number of seahorse sightings since the pandemic when a fall in the number of boats visiting the Dorset beauty spot allowed recovery.

Hoping for the upward trend to continue divers have been in the water every two weeks.

"Without a doubt every dive we're seeing seahorses" says founder of The Seahorse Trust, Neil Garrick-Maidment.

"At one stage we went through two and a half years without a single sea horse sighting here."

"It's difficult to know long term what the trend of numbers is. The other fish species like the bass and stuff are breeding quite well here so – yeah – fingers crossed – we're being really optimistic about what's going on."

That optimism is built on the formation of the Studland Bay Marine Partnership and the introduction of the eco moorings initiative which prevents chains scraping the seabed and seagrass when boats visit the bay.

Currently there are 87 moorings in the bay with plans to install more in the future.

The ongoing survey work is done under strict conditions. It's illegal to disturb or harm seahorses.

Anyone intending to film, photograph or survey seahorses has to be licensed.

For volunteers like Kat Lewis encounters with the creature are still magical.

"We found two baby ones. So yeah – good – two baby ones and three cuttlefish. Loads and loads of little dragonets and wrasse and all the usual suspects."

"Why would you not want to see seahorses? They're kind of like unicorns of the sea."

Former BBC journalist Angus Crawford joined the volunteers after being inspired by the trust's work.

"I found three seahorses. One tiny – just a small fry from this year. Then a bigger female. And then the most beautiful, enormous seahorse. The biggest I've ever seen here."

But while the numbers of encounters seems promising there is a note of caution.

Studland's seagrass is found in shallow water leaving it vulnerable to winter storms.

Climate experts are predicting the UK could see winter storms increasing in number and intensity.

"This bay is wonderful" explains Ken Collins, senior research fellow, from the University of Southampton

"It's protected from prevailing south westerly winds which is why the seagrass grows here, the boaters like it – you know – they get shelter."

"But in some years – we had a lot of easterly winds which blow straight into the bay. The can actually tear up the seagrass. And so unpredictable weather – storminess – is a concern."

While seahorses retreat to deep waters in the winter healthy seagrass meadows are vital to their breeding cycle.

For now though at Studland the signs are encouraging and for the volunteers every encounter is still magical.

articles.title: UK government invests £30m in Shetland spaceport
articles.summary: The funding will be used to build two more launchpads.
articles.body:
The UK government has announced investment of £30m in SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland as part of a new national space strategy.

A spaceport spokesperson said the funding was a "hugely significant" vote of confidence and would unlock a further £30m of private investment.

Several companies hope to use SaxaVord in Unst, the northernmost point in the UK, as a launch site for small commercial rockets.

A government spokesperson said space was "an increasingly important domain" for keeping the country safe.

SaxaVord is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport and has regulatory approval for up to 30 rocket launches a year.

The company said the £60m public-private investment package would be used to design and build a second hangar and two more launchpads.

Chief executive officer Scott Hammond said the funding would take the company to the next stage of its development.

"We are building the spaceport for the thousandth as much as the first launch," he said.

"We're trying to create a successful, safe and sustainable business. This is direct investment into Shetland."

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

Two German companies have signed launch agreements with the spaceport.

Rocket Factory Augsburg (RFA) is working towards its first vertical orbital test flight from UK soil. In August, SaxaVord paused plans for a test launch after RFA said it had "encountered an issue".

A five-week "launch window" had been due to begin, with temporary traffic restrictions introduced in the event of a flight attempt.

A second company, HyImpulse Technologies GmbH (HyImpulse), plans the second flight of its SR75 suborbital launch vehicle from Shetland this year.

The German firm recently secured investment of more than €50m (£43m).

Derek Harris, head of programmes at Space Scotland, said he was not concerned about the timescale of the launch, adding that the £30m investment was a "good starter".

"The technology is difficult to master but you would prefer it to be there and be reliable so if the timescale slips into next year, I do not see that as a failure," he told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast .

"I see that as a very well-maintained programme to make sure health and safety and reliability are at the forefront."

Harris said rain and storms could also impact the process and it was important to remain open minded.

He added: "It will take time and a lot of money but once it launches, the benefits it unlocks for Scotland and the UK will be amazing."

SaxaVord Spaceport has confirmed that it is in discussions with other companies.

The UK government said the new space strategy would "drive growth, strengthen security and back the technologies that underpin modern life".

Ministers said they wanted to create jobs and help Britain and its partners launch satellites without relying on countries "further afield".

The money for the Shetland project is part of a £148m investment across Europe which ministers said would help UK space technology firms secure more work.

Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander said: "Scotland already builds more satellites than anywhere else in Europe, and with a £30m UK government investment boost, SaxaVord is now poised to deliver up to three-quarters of the continent's orbital launch slots."

He added that defence, security and economic growth were at the heart of the plan.

Lise Kaae, chief executive of Heartland, which has a majority stake in SaxaVord Spaceport through its investment arm Wild Ventures, said: "We are very pleased to welcome the UK government as an investor and partner."

The investment is subject to due diligence and final sign-off.

articles.summary: Middle East News: Dubai: Iran said it will announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, along with maps of a new shipping corridor through the Strait .
articles.body: Dubai: Iran said it will announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, along with maps of a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, as a weekend exchange of strikes on shipping sent oil prices higher on Monday. The new restricted zone will begin from where the US blockade of Iran begins and extend into areas of the Gulf, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Sunday in an interview with state TV.Few details were provided on the plan, but Rezaei said any ship entering the new zone would be added to a sanctions list.In addition, maps detailing passage routes for the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit largely closed to tanker traffic, would also be approved soon, Rezaei said. “The maps of a new international corridor which lies in Iranian and Omani waters and in which Iran will have management have been agreed and should be signed in the coming days,” he said.“We will only commit to the Strait of Hormuz being open when they (the Americans) stop the sabotage, threats and attacks on Iran,” Rezaei added.Iran govt to raise fuel price for heavy users: Iran will raise the price of gasoline for users surpassing 110 litres per month starting Tuesday, a govt spokesperson said Sunday.The price of the first and second quotas, which include 110 litres, will remain unchanged, but the price of the third quota will be raised to 100,000 Iranian rials per litre (around 4 US cents based on the free-market rate), Fatemeh Mohajerani said in comments carried by state media. The increase in Iran’s gasoline price, which is one of the lowest in the world, was discussed by the govt and postponed amid concerns it could trigger new protests. Iran experienced widespread protests in 2019 over the same issue. articles.title: 'Unprecedented wildfires' in Essex leads to busy summer for crews
articles.summary: A senior firefighter thanks Essex residents for their support during a busy summer.
articles.body:
An "unprecedented number of wildfires" led to one of Essex County Fire and Rescue Service's busiest ever summers, it has said.

Crews responded to more than 4,200 incidents across July and August, compared to 3,821 during the same months in 2025.

Large-scale emergencies included an explosion in Rettendon , which injured 20 firefighters, and flames twice breaking out at Middlewick Ranges in Colchester .

Area manager Dave Bond said thousands of people had sent crews messages of support and thanks for their work.

"When residents take the time to see how they can help during incidents or to share their thanks afterwards, it provides a real boost to morale," Bond said.

The summer of 2026 was the UK's hottest on record , according to provisional data from the Met Office.

The dry conditions led to fires breaking out in fields and spreading quickly.

In the week to 30 July, the fire service received 2,029 emergency calls and dispatched crews to 570 incidents.

They also supported colleagues in Suffolk when flames engulfed an area the size of 210 football pitches at Dunwich Heath .

"Throughout this hot and very dry summer, we've received thousands of messages from residents asking how they can help, thanking our crews, and offering words of support and encouragement," Bond said.

articles.title: Lightning struck an 1890 Georgia mansion; its owners drove away unaware the turret was burning until passersby spotted flames, and firefighters kept the main floor undamaged
articles.summary: US News: A lightning strike set fire to the turret of a historic Georgia mansion Saturday night, damaging its distinctive steeple and balcony but leaving the b.
articles.body: A lightning strike set fire to the turret of a historic Georgia mansion Saturday night, damaging its distinctive steeple and balcony but leaving the business operating inside largely untouched, according to FOX 5 Atlanta, which reported the incident on September 6. The fire broke out at the Maple Street Mansion at 401 Maple Street in Carrollton after lightning struck the building during a severe storm. The mansion, which dates to 1890, currently houses The Heirloom Store, a retail business run by owners Rhett and Malina. The Heirloom Store’s own account of the property confirms the mansion was built in 1890 and has served as a landmark in Carrollton for more than a century.Owners did not know the mansion had caught fireThe incident unfolded as the owners waited out the storm nearby. According to the account shared by the owners and reported by FOX 5 Atlanta, Rhett and Malina had been parked outside as the weather worsened when a powerful lightning bolt struck. They did not initially realize that the historic building had been hit.They briefly went inside after noticing flickering lights, resetting a breaker before leaving the property. By then, however, the lightning strike had ignited the upper portion of the mansion. It was passersby who noticed flames coming from the roof and called 911, bringing emergency crews to the property before the fire could spread further.Fire contained to the turretFirefighters were able to confine the blaze to the mansion’s upper exterior. The turret and steeple sustained significant structural damage, as did the balcony. But the fire did not make its way down into the main floor, where The Heirloom Store operates.The owners said the store’s merchandise and main-floor interior escaped both fire and water damage. That distinction is particularly significant for the historic property, which has been used for commercial purposes for decades. The Heirloom Store describes the building as a roughly 33,000-square-foot landmark with a history stretching back to its construction by L.C. Mandeville in the late 19th century. The property has housed restaurants, event spaces and other businesses over the years.A historic Carrollton landmarkThe Maple Street Mansion is more than a commercial property in Carrollton. The Victorian-era building is closely tied to the city’s history and was originally the home of L.C. Mandeville, an influential businessman associated with Mandeville Mills. Historical records held by the University of West Georgia identify the property at 401 Maple Street as the L.C. Mandeville House and document its significance to Carrollton’s development.The building also survived a potential demolition in 2014, according to The Heirloom Store’s history of the property, before entering another chapter as a retail and community space.Repairs planned as business continuesWhile the visible damage is concentrated high above the main floor, the full extent of the lightning strike’s impact has not yet been established. A detailed inspection was expected once crews could safely examine the structure in daylight, particularly for electrical damage that may not be immediately visible.For now, the owners intend to begin exterior repairs while keeping The Heirloom Store open. What began with a lightning strike could therefore have ended very differently. Instead, a blaze high in the mansion’s iconic turret was spotted in time, firefighters stopped it from descending into the building, and the business below was left standing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Instagram users face ransom demands over fake copyright claims
articles.summary: Users say they are losing money or risk having their accounts suspended because Meta struggles to identify scammers.
articles.body:
Instagram creators say they have lost thousands of pounds after their accounts were suspended or taken down due to fake copyright claims.

Extorters have filed bogus claims to the Meta-owned social media platform, then asked for ransoms to withdraw them - knowing repeated claims can lead to account bans.

One Instagram user, who has 1.5 million followers, told the BBC he paid a scammer $50 (£37) to get his account back, claiming Meta's appeal process would take weeks, which had previously cost him thousands in lost income.

"We understand this can be frustrating for those impacted, and our systems are designed to protect people from this happening in the first place," a Meta spokesperson said.

"Following our review, we have restored the affected content and added additional protections to safeguard accounts against further attempts of this kind."

However, content creators the BBC has spoken to say Meta is poor at identifying obviously spurious cases, and say its appeals process is slow to respond unless you pay a monthly fee.

The Lost in Time History Instagram account posts historical pictures to its more than 1.5 million followers.

Its creator Olly, who did not share his last name, told the BBC he posts pictures in the public domain or where he has permission from the rights holder.

Yet he has received dozens of "obviously fake" copyright complaints so far in 2026.

Meta does not check the authenticity of complaints when they are made, so if someone is hit repeatedly, their account can be temporarily taken down.

Olly says he often gets struck for multiple posts at a time, all from the same email address.

He then gets contacted by the person asking to go on to the private messaging app Telegram.

"They'll demand a certain amount of money," he said - usually amounting to a few hundred dollars - to withdraw the claim.

The BBC has seen messages from the claimants where they demand money or threaten future copyright strikes.

Olly ultimately agreed to pay an extorter $50 in cryptocurrency to restore his account, which had been temporarily taken down by Instagram.

Law enforcement organisations tell extortion victims not to pay ransoms as it fuels the criminal ecosystem.

Olly said he paid as a "last resort" because it was quicker than going through Meta, which could take weeks.

But he was hit by more copyright strikes immediately after he paid.

"Having to pay the person who's actively put you through all of that anguish only for it to happen straight away again."

As a result of the number of times he has been hit by copyright claims, Olly's account was demonetised, meaning he could not earn money from Instagram for high-performing posts.

"There's no investigation into abuse, or system detection [from Meta] that it could be abuse," he said.

Other Instagram users have shared similar experiences.

"Meta was not helpful throughout the entire process, forcing you to pay for support to talk, even as they claim to be here for the creator," said Abin Tom Sebastian, who is behind the Morbid Kuriosity account.

Meta charges a £9.99 monthly fee to be Verified on Instagram, which gives users 24/7 access to support via a live chat.

"I lost irrecoverable and crucial, brand contracts that unfortunately moved ahead with another creator, and no reassurance or support from Meta saying this will not happen again," Sebastian said.

Instagram says only copyright holders, or an authorised representative, can report copyright infringement, and it advises affected users to contacted rights holders directly.

After the BBC contacted Meta with examples from Olly and other account holders, Meta said it had applied additional protections to their accounts, which it said would prevent similar issues happening in the future.

It said it fought against deceptive behaviour to scam or defraud people and businesses.

The BBC has spoken to three people who file copyright strikes against Instagram users, despite not being the copyright holders.

All three appear to be based in India, or in countries nearby.

They deny they are holding accounts to ransom - instead saying they file legitimate claims on behalf of copyright holders.

But the BBC has seen messages from one where they ask for $900 (£668) to withdraw a strike.

They claimed this was their payment for the service, and confirmed they kept all the money.

Two others denied they made any money at all.

One said they are sent accounts to target and investigate the claim.

"If I find that they are using someone else's content, I issue copyright strikes for the benefit of everyone," they said.

The other said they are sent accounts or posts via an account holder or another representative.

Legitimate agencies do exist which are paid to file copyright strikes on behalf of clients.

But Olly - who has dealt with these before when he has mistakenly posted copyrighted material - says they are usually easy to deal with, and "you can easily tell the difference".

"They're established companies with millions of followers, so it's very different," he said.

These kinds of copyright scams are not new, with a version of the crime dating back to the early days of the internet, said Andres Guadamuz, reader in intellectual property law of the University of Sussex and an expert on digital copyright.

Previously, they were emails or letters sent to website owners claiming they owned the copyright to photos used online, and asking for money to avoid legal action.

Similar strikes have been used against YouTube users too .

But the recent increase in this method may be because AI has made it easier to do this on a larger scale.

"It's a numbers game," Guadamuz told the BBC.

"Pretty much anyone can now deploy [AI] that is going to automate all of this in some way," he said.

It is also harder for the platforms - with billions of users - to police the racket, and distinguish the real copyright claims from the fake ones.

"The system was almost built with the assumption that the person that was making a copyright strike claim was legitimate," he said.

articles.title: Meet Celine Zhang, the 18-year-old New Jersey student who developed a way to prove a digital puzzle was solved without revealing the answer
articles.summary: US News: Think of a situation where you are working on a challenging puzzle when someone asks you to demonstrate that you’ve solved it, but you can’t show them.
articles.body: Think of a situation where you are working on a challenging puzzle when someone asks you to demonstrate that you’ve solved it, but you can’t show them your work. That sounds like near impossibility. But for 18-year-old Celine Zhang of Princeton, New Jersey, that challenge became the foundation for an innovative computer science project: building a better robot. According to a report by Society for Science, Zhang’s computer science project at the Regeneron Science Talent Search was based on a mathematical idea called zero-knowledge proofs. These are techniques that allow a person to prove to someone else that they know something without revealing the knowledge, mentions the report. Zhang realized the idea in puzzle games with a moving avatar that fuses blocks. Her method allows a player who has solved a puzzle to prove that they know the solution without just giving it away to another player. Instead of giving away the entire answer, the solver might offer some particular, but limited, guidance that lets others check off the achievement. The idea is that it gives you the ability to build trust without giving away the solution .From games to cyber securityThough the project is based on puzzles, Zhang’s work has applications far beyond games. The same principles that underlie her approach could potentially be useful in fields like digital security, machine learning, and blockchain authentication, where it can be valuable to prove that someone has the right information without revealing sensitive data. Her project demonstrates how an abstract mathematical concept can be tied to real-world problems in technology, transforming an ordinary question about puzzles into an investigation of privacy and authentication.A student with many interestsZhang is a student at Phillips Exeter Academy and is co-head of the engineering club and co-leader of the Junior Computer Programming Club. Through the programming club, she teaches beginning computer science to elementary and middle school students in the Exeter area. Her interests extend beyond the realm of technology. Zhang is the section leader for the sopranos in PEADQUACS, a co-ed a cappella group that performs at school showcases, admissions events and community gatherings.Beyond the projectZhang also serves as an instructor and teaching assistant at AlphaStar Academy where he teaches computer science classes and helps students with their questions. She enjoys being game-ready when she’s not working on computer science or music. Fun fact about her? Zhang always has a deck of cards with her, in case she can play the strategy game Avalon with a friend.Images Courtesy: Society for Science and istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: U.K. to sanction Israeli West Bank settlements, setting up clash with U.S.
articles.summary: Britain will announce a trade ban on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank later on Tuesday, a senior minister said, framed as a step up in UK support for a two-state solution.
articles.body: Britain will announce a trade ban on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank later on Tuesday, a senior minister said, framed as a step up in UK support for a two-state solution. The U.S. is likely to strongly oppose Britain’s intervention, and some in Israel have already reacted angrily with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich calling for the UK ambassador to be expelled. Britain’s foreign minister Ed Miliband, six weeks into the job, flagged last week that he wanted to reset policy on Israel and he will announce the trading restrictions later. The impact on the £6 billion ($8.12 billion) of annual bilateral trade is likely to be minimal, with details unclear of how the UK will differentiate between goods originating in West Bank settlements from products made in Israel. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, in office since July, discussed the Middle East in a call with President Donald Trump on Monday, when he stressed “the importance of the two-state solution”, according to his office. At issue is Israel’s E1 settlement project in the West Bank, which Miliband and other western politicians have said would cut across land the Palestinians seek for their own state. U.N. bodies and most governments, including Britain, consider Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal and regard the West Bank as territory under military occupation. Israel says the territory is disputed rather than occupied, and asserts that Jews have a historical claim to the land. Britain and other European nations criticized Israel’s E1 settlement plans in August, and work and pensions minister Pat McFadden said these developments were behind the sanctions. “The reason that danger has become more urgent is because of expanded settlement activity in recent weeks and months,” he said on Times Radio on Tuesday. The Israeli prime minister’s office and foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing an election on October 27, with polls showing his ruling coalition is likely to lose several seats and fall short of a majority. Israel-UK relations have become increasingly strained in recent years with London criticising Israel’s conduct in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank and rising settler attacks on Palestinians. Spain, Ireland and the Netherlands have each moved to ban imports of goods originating in Israeli settlements in the West Bank, though not all the bans have come into effect. McFadden said on Sky News that Israel would remain an important trading partner for the UK and there would not be a boycott of all Israeli goods. Goods originating from settlements are mainly agricultural, including fresh produce and wine, and make up only a tiny fraction of Israel’s total trade flows. Foreign diplomats say an import ban could be difficult to enforce as some goods from Israel may use products from settlements without identifying their origin.

articles.title: In 2014, Verona removed its bronze Juliet statue after years of touching for luck in love; repeated handling left cracks and wear that made it unfit for display
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The iconic bronze Juliet statue in Verona, renowned for bringing love luck to touch, has been removed due to excessive wear and tear; explore the tale of its replacement and preservation.
articles.body: For more than 40 years, people visiting Casa di Giulietta in Verona used to line up in the courtyard to touch the bronze statue of Juliet's right breast, a gesture believed to bring good fortune in matters of love. In 2014, city authorities decided to remove the statue from the site because its structure had deteriorated, making it unfit to display in public. The statue was installed in the courtyard in 1972. It was created by Veronese sculptor Nereo Costantini in 1969 and donated by the Verona Lions Club, according to Verona's official tourism pages.Millions of tourists visit the same small spot of bronzeCasa di Giulietta's courtyard is one of the most visited spots in Verona, according to Verona's tourism office, and visitors often deliberately touch the same point on the statue, believed to bring luck in love. This kind of wear differs from ordinary weathering, since natural exposure affects a bronze surface evenly, while repeated touching erodes one small area far faster than the rest. By 2013, city officials confirmed the statue had sustained significant wear on its right side, arm, and breast, where a crack had also formed beneath the surface. Assessments concluded the damage was too extensive for the statue to safely remain in the courtyard for continued public handling, so officials opted to cast a new statue rather than attempt a repair.Building a replica from a silicone mold of the originalThe replacement sculpture was installed in the courtyard toward the end of June 2014. The project had a budget of approximately €15,000, supplied by the Italian insurance company Società Cattolica di Assicurazione. The new statue was cast at the Fonderia Brustolin foundry under the direction of Rodolfo Camatta, using a silicone mold taken from the original bronze. According to Verona's museum authority, sculptor Novello Finotti, a former student of Costantini, returned to serve as a consultant on the casting.Rather than scrapping the damaged original, city authorities moved it indoors to the Casa di Giulietta complex, where it remains on display, protected from further handling. Visitors can still view the worn breast and cracked arm up close, though only through the museum's glass display case, not by direct contact. The custom of touching the statue's right breast for luck in love has no documented origin tied to a specific person, historical figure, or organization. It appears to have developed organically among visitors sometime after the statue's installation in 1972.What Verona learned from the replacementAs PBS NewsHour reported around the time of the statue's removal, Giulio Tamassia of the Juliet Club had warned for years about the sculpture's deterioration. City officials made no design changes in 2014 to protect the new sculpture from the same kind of wear, since the statue's appeal depends on direct public contact rather than distant viewing. Verona has not proposed installing a barrier or discouraging the touching tradition, suggesting the city has accepted periodic replacement as the practical cost of preserving a custom that has become part of the site's identity.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ICE crackdown laid bare at Venice festival documentary
articles.summary: Oscar-winning filmmaker Laura Poitras said she ​hopes a new documentary about U.S. immigration raids will help “denormalize” violence under President Donald Trump’s ‌mass deportation campaign.
articles.body: VENICE — Oscar-winning filmmaker Laura Poitras said on Monday she ​hopes a new documentary about U.S. immigration raids will help “denormalize” violence under President Donald Trump’s ‌mass deportation campaign. Premiering at the Venice Film Festival, the 25-minute documentary “They’re Here”, co-directed by Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller, follows volunteers in Minneapolis as they track the movements of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents conducting deportation operations earlier this year. “The reality is a ​nightmare. The entire country is under attack and immigrants are living in fear throughout the ​United States right now,” Poitras said ahead of the screening. Confronting protesters in the snow Trump ⁠launched his deportation drive immediately after taking office in January 2025. He has defended ICE’s tactics and ​argued that people who entered the U.S. illegally must be sent home. The Minneapolis sweep drew weeks of demonstrations ​and confrontations between protesters and ICE agents in which immigration officers shot dead two U.S. citizens. “In the mainstream media, this kind of violence is being normalized. We believe very strongly in the power of cinema to denormalize this violence and to ​show what’s happening,” Poitras told a news conference. Poitras, whose full-length documentary “All the Beauty and the Bloodshed,” won Venice’s ​top Golden Lion prize in 2022, said she and Mueller decided to make a much shorter film because they felt ‌it ⁠was urgent to show immediately what was happening. Shot largely from the perspective of local residents tracking the movements of ICE teams, “They’re Here” cuts between volunteer dispatch networks and the story of a Mexican man hiding from immigration authorities with the help of his son. The documentary shows locals plotting the routes of unmarked ICE cars, ​masked agents confronting protesters on ​snow-covered streets and handcuffed ⁠detainees boarding deportation flights. Community Response The Minneapolis crackdown became one of the flashpoints in the broader deportation campaign and the U.S. administration eventually scaled back the operation after ​months of unrest. Mueller said the filmmakers wanted to document both the scope of ​the anti-migrant sweep ⁠and the community response it provoked across the city. “The resistance remained one of documentation more than anything else, precisely because it was about keeping people safe rather than fighting ICE,” she said. “These are our neighbors, and we ⁠don’t want ​them stolen from us.” She said the eventual drawdown on ICE ​operatives showed that the community action had worked. “ICE removed 80% of its agents. So there was a real response to this kind of ​resistance, which I think we can all take hope from,” she said.

articles.title: In 1997, Texas researchers poured fluorescein into Dry Fork Sink to map Austin’s hidden aquifer; it travelled at least 4.8 miles to Barton Springs in under 30 hours
articles.summary: US News: In a groundbreaking study, Texas researchers injected fluorescein into Dry Fork Sink, uncovering a rapid 4.5-mile water connection to Barton Springs in under 30 hours. This innovative technique sheds light on the Edwards Aquifer's surprising groundwater flow dynamics and has crucial implications for water quality management.
articles.body: To understand where water was travelling beneath Austin, researchers used a technique that could make an invisible journey visible. According to the Barton Springs/Edwards Aquifer Conservation District, researchers injected three pounds of fluorescein dye into Dry Fork Sink on June 17, 1997, at 9 am. The sink is located on Kitcheon Branch, a tributary of Williamson Creek, in Sunset Valley, and was used as a natural recharge feature of the Edwards Aquifer. Researchers poured the dye into water entering the sinkhole and later detected it at Barton Springs, demonstrating a rapid underground connection. The report notes that fluorescein was one of several non-toxic organic dyes selected for groundwater tracing because of its suitability and safety for drinking-water supplies and aquatic habitats.A dye trail beneath the cityThe fluorescein travelled underground and was detected at Barton Springs in under 30 hours. The original tracing report gives the minimum distance to the detection point as about 4.8 miles, while an accompanying account puts it at 4.5 miles. Either way, the experiment demonstrated a rapid connection between Dry Fork Sink and the springs. This result mattered because the Edwards Aquifer does not behave like a conventional underground reservoir, where water seeps slowly through tiny spaces between sediment grains. It is a karst system carved into limestone that has fractured and dissolved over geological time. Water can therefore find preferential routes through openings and interconnected conduits, allowing it to travel much faster than might be expected from ordinary groundwater movement.According to research published in the Journal of Contemporary Water Research & Education, a long-distance groundwater-tracing programme began in 1996 and used injected tracers to map groundwater basins and underground flow paths in the Barton Springs segment of the Edwards Aquifer. Results from 40 groundwater traces, 88% of which were successfully recovered, showed that groundwater can move rapidly through the karst aquifer, with mean residence times of about one to eight days. The study found that tracer pulses travelled through conduit pathways far more rapidly than through the aquifer's diffuse-flow component, demonstrating how quickly water can move between recharge areas and springs under suitable conditions.An underground map made with colourThe Dry Fork test was one of many in a broader series that began in the mid-1990s to understand how water enters the aquifer and moves underground before reaching springs or other discharge points. Monitoring equipment was installed at the spring sites and other places where the dye could be found. The activated charcoal receptors proved especially helpful because they could capture traces of the dye, while water samples provided further readings on the tracer. The wider programme eventually identified several groundwater basins within the Barton Springs segment. Traces from parts of the Williamson and Barton Creek watersheds were shown to move toward different discharge points, including Barton Springs and Cold Springs. This replaced assumptions about underground water movement with evidence from water moving through the aquifer.The speed observed at Dry Fork Sink was impressive. Three pounds of fluorescein had to travel at least several miles within less than a day and a quarter. The estimated initial velocity exceeded 21,100 feet per day, but that figure should be treated as a minimum estimate rather than the true speed of water through all underground passages. The water does not follow a simple direct path between sink and spring. The experiment also shows why dye tracing is so useful in a karst aquifer. Underground pathways cannot be identified from surface geology alone. Dye introduced at one point allows groundwater to carry that information downstream.Why Austin's hidden water mattersBarton Springs is more than a picturesque landmark. It is a major discharge site in the Barton Springs portion of the Edwards Aquifer and has played an important role in Austin's hydrology for many years. The springs are habitat for endangered aquatic species, so groundwater quality is both a management and ecological issue. That is why the understanding of the groundwater flow paths is so vital. If water can travel from a sinkhole to a spring in hours rather than months or years, contaminants in the recharge area may reach groundwater much faster than expected.Research published in the Journal of Contemporary Water Research & Education also notes that the broader tracing programme demonstrated that rapid groundwater movement is a defining feature of parts of the Barton Springs system. A later synthesis of the tracing work reported that dozens of groundwater traces had been used to delineate flow paths and groundwater basins, with rapid travel times repeatedly observed under suitable conditions. Thus, the Dry Fork Sink experiment made underground flow visible and showed that water entering the sinkhole in the Williamson Creek basin could reach Barton Springs in just a few hours.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: We want to hear how Medicaid caregiving cuts are affecting you
articles.summary: This article is part of “Disabled and Denied,” a series examining cuts to Medicaid home care and the fallout for disabled people and their families.
articles.body: This article is part of “Disabled and Denied,” a series examining cuts to Medicaid home care and the fallout for disabled people and their families. NBC News is looking to speak to people who rely on Medicaid-funded care at home, as well as family members, workers and advocates who support them. For decades, Medicaid home- and community-based services have helped millions of disabled and older Americans live independently rather than in institutions or nursing facilities. Now, a series of changes at the state and federal levels is threatening that system. President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by nearly $1 trillion over the next decade. Conservative officials and activists have increasingly portrayed home care as wasteful and rife with fraud. And the Justice Department has backed away from the federal government’s long-standing interpretation of a landmark Supreme Court ruling protecting the right of disabled people to receive services in their communities. The Trump administration denies that it’s targeting disability programs, arguing that its efforts to root out waste and abuse will protect Medicaid for vulnerable Americans who need it. The biggest federal cuts won’t begin to hit until next year, but the system is already showing signs of strain. In some states, officials have cut wages or capped hours for paid family caregivers. Fraud crackdowns have jeopardized care for families who say they did nothing wrong. And some disabled people have had their caregiving slashed by new algorithmic assessments. For families who depend on these programs, the stakes are profound. Many fear the changes will unravel a fragile system built over generations to help disabled and older Americans live outside of institutions. articles.title: U.S. Coast Guard joins Bahamas search for missing plane carrying 4 family members
articles.summary: A small plane carrying four family members flying back home to Florida went missing off the Bahamas on Monday, authorities said.
articles.body: A small plane carrying four family members flying back home to Florida went missing off the Bahamas on Monday, the U.S. Coast Guard and authorities in the Bahamas said. The plane took off from Great Harbour Cay and was heading to Miami Executive Airport in Miami-Dade County, Bahamas police said in a statement. “Police on the island of Andros are coordinating efforts to locate an aircraft believed to have crash-landed off the coast of Red Bays, North Andros,” the agency said. Silvia Larrieu said her uncle, Mario Lamar, was piloting the plane. In a video statement shared by WSVN-TV in Miami, Larrieu said that the plane was also carrying Lamar’s wife Lily Lamar and two of his grandchildren, Christian Sosa and Sophie Sosa. Larrieu pleaded with anyone who can help to assist in the search. “Whether it’s by plane, by boat, any signs that you’ve noticed, to help us find them and bring them back alive,” said Larrieu. Bahamas police identified the plane as a PA-34 Piper five-seater aircraft, with tail number N212ML. It said it departed Great Harbour Cay, a city in the Berry Islands of the Bahamas. Air traffic control lost contact with the aircraft when it was about 13 miles west of Andros Island, Bahamas police said. Bahamian officials contacted the U.S. Coast Guard at about 2 p.m. and requested assistance finding a downed plane, a spokesperson said. “Southeast District command center watchstanders coordinated the launch of an HC-144 Ocean Sentry to assist Bahamian authorities with the search,” the spokesperson said. The search had to be suspended due to bad weather, Bahamas police said. It was not clear when it would resume.

articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian president Vladimir Putin are scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting on Friday, with trade and econo.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian president Vladimir Putin are scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting on Friday, with trade and economic cooperation expected to feature prominently on the agenda, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.Moscow also welcomed India’s willingness to contribute to efforts aimed at finding a peaceful resolution to the Ukraine conflict.Putin is scheduled to visit India for the BRICS Summit, which will begin in New Delhi on September 12. Ahead of the visit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the trip will provide an opportunity for the two countries to discuss issues concerning bilateral relations. He also wished India success in hosting the summit."In a couple of days, President Putin will begin his India visit. You know that our two leaders, Indian and Russian leaders, are in a very close personal contact. They are very pragmatic in their relationship, and they are as sincere as to be able to discuss in a very open and constructive way the most sensitive issues of our agenda and our bilateral relations. Of course, it opens additional horizons for our cooperation," Peskov said."We have no doubt that the summit will be successful. Russia, we are doing our best to contribute to further development of BRICS cooperation in the three main pillars of our interaction. So, those are policy and security. economy and finance, and cultural and humanitarian contexts. So, we are supporting idea of inviting new countries to join different formats within BRICS," he added.Peskov said Russia is awaiting negotiations with India on setting up new nuclear power plants, adding that the sale of Su-57 fighter aircraft to India is also on the agenda.The Kremlin spokesperson stressed the need for cooperation in the financial sector, alleging that some countries were using their currencies as a tool of political oppression."The cooperation space within Brics financial sphere is of great importance. Russia recently reached a level of 90 percent of all the payments, all the transactions with Brics countries being made in national currencies, it's very important. It's not because we are aiming for de-dollarization, for getting rid of US dollars. To the contrary, we are open to to every acceptable methods of payments, but you know that certain countries are using some national currencies as a tool for political oppression. They are introducing sanctions based on their national currencies. So, if they don't let us use their money, we use our own money," Peskov said.India is set to host the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13, 2026, as the grouping of major emerging market economies and developing nations continues to expand its role in global affairs.The grouping began as Bric, comprising Brazil, Russia, India and China. It held its first Foreign Ministers’ meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in 2006, followed by its inaugural summit in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009. South Africa joined the grouping in 2011, leading to the formation of BRICS.Under India’s 2026 chairship theme, “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” New Delhi is seeking to move the grouping’s agenda beyond political coordination towards practical cooperation in areas including trade, agriculture, healthcare, energy, digital technology, urban development, small enterprises, startups, climate action and cultural exchanges.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Woman divorced after father's death can get his family pension, Tripura HC rules
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Tripura high court has directed the Agartala Municipal Corporation to pay family pension to a divorced daughter from the date she obtai.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Tripura high court has directed the Agartala Municipal Corporation to pay family pension to a divorced daughter from the date she obtained her divorce, ruling that she could not be denied the benefit merely because she was still married when her pensioner father died. The court directed the corporation to pay her pension from October 4, 2021, with arrears and 6 percent interest.Why was the woman's family pension claim rejected?According to the August 18 order, Ujjwala Rani Paul was the daughter of an Agartala Municipal Corporation employee who retired in 2004 and died on December 2, 2018. However, his wife had already died.Paul had been married to Pradip Saha when her father died. She later obtained a mutual-consent divorce from him on October 4, 2021. She applied for family pension on February 23, 2022, under the Tripura State Civil Services (Revised Pension) Rules, 2017.The corporation rejected her claim in October 2024, saying a 2018 memorandum extending family pension benefits to divorced daughters of pensioners had not been adopted and ratified by it.Paul challenged the decision before the high court. The single judge agreed that the pension rules covered divorced daughters but rejected her claim on the ground that she was not divorced when her father died.What did the high court find about her eligibility?A division bench comprising Chief Justice M.S. Ramachandra Rao and Justice Biswajit Palit found that the corporation's position was contrary to its own records. The corporation had itself stated that a legally divorced daughter was entitled to family pension under Rule 8, subject to the income condition.The bench also noted that Paul had been living with and dependent on her father for years. Her divorce petition stated that her husband had left shortly after their marriage in 1982 and that she had taken shelter in her father's home.The court said the rules did not specifically require a daughter to be divorced on the date her father died.“Neither Rule 8 quoted above nor the amendment to the CCS (Pension) Rules, 1972 states explicitly that to claim the benefit of Family Pension, the daughter of the pensioner should be a divorcee at the time of his death,” the court said.The bench held that the single judge had therefore added a condition that was not present in the rules. It said the right to family pension arises on the death of the pensioner or the pensioner's spouse receiving the pension.“When such a requirement is not provided in the applicable rule, in our opinion, the learned Single Judge erred in reading such a requirement into Rule 8,” the court held.The high court also referred to a 2017 Government of India memorandum which allowed family pension to a divorced daughter even where divorce proceedings had been filed during the pensioner's lifetime but the divorce took place after his death.The bench said this showed that a daughter did not necessarily have to be divorced when her father died to qualify for the benefit. It also noted that the pension rules were intended to provide financial support to dependent family members.The court rejected the corporation's attempt to cast doubt on Paul's claim that her husband had left her shortly after their marriage. It said there was no reason to doubt the statement because her former husband had also agreed to it.“It is unfortunate that such an unfair stand has been taken by the Agartala Municipal Corporation,” the court observed.The bench then allowed Paul's appeal and set aside the April 1, 2026 judgment of the single judge.It directed the Agartala Municipal Corporation to pay her family pension from October 4, 2021, the date she obtained the divorce decree, and continue paying it during her lifetime.The corporation was also directed to pay all arrears within three months, along with 6 percent annual interest calculated from the respective dates on which the pension amounts became due until payment.

articles.title: Robin Williams built a 640-acre Napa estate with a 20,000-sq-ft mansion; after years on the market, it sold for $18.1 million after being listed for $35 million
articles.summary: US News: Robin Williams' Napa Valley estate, known as Villa Sorriso, was an extraordinary private retreat that combined a vast mountain property with a mansion.
articles.body: Robin Williams' Napa Valley estate, known as Villa Sorriso, was an extraordinary private retreat that combined a vast mountain property with a mansion of nearly 20,000 square feet. Williams commissioned the estate in the early 2000s, creating a secluded compound spread across about 640 acres in the Mayacamas Mountains between Napa and Sonoma valleys. The property included vineyards, olive trees, a swimming pool, tennis court, horse facilities and extensive trails, while the main house featured luxury spaces including a library, theatre, wine and art storage and multiple bedrooms. Williams first put the estate on the market in 2012 for $35 million, but it did not find a buyer. After several price reductions and years on the market, Villa Sorriso eventually sold in January 2016 for $18.1 million in cash, about half the original asking price.How Robin Williams built his 640-acre Napa retreatWilliams commissioned Villa Sorriso in the early 2000s and built the property as a private retreat in the Mayacamas Mountains. The estate was named Villa Sorriso, meaning "Villa of Smiles", and was positioned between Napa and Sonoma valleys. The main residence was a limestone-clad mansion covering nearly 20,000 square feet. Its scale was matched by the surrounding land, which included more than 18 acres of producing vineyards, mature olive trees, hiking and horse-riding trails, a spring-fed pond and a nine-stall horse barn. The estate also included a caretaker's house with four bedrooms. The combination of the enormous acreage, vineyards and secluded mountain setting made the property considerably more than a conventional celebrity home.What was inside Robin Williams' 20,000-square-foot mansionThe mansion was designed as an elaborate entertainment and family retreat, with five bedrooms and 10 bathrooms in the main house. Inside were a two-storey entrance with a rotunda and bell tower, an oak-panelled library, a billiards room and a 12-seat home theatre. The property also contained three safe rooms and an elevator serving all three floors. Climate-controlled cellars provided storage for wine and artwork. Outside, the grounds featured a 65-foot infinity-edge swimming pool, tennis court, lawns and landscaped gardens. The property also offered sweeping views of the surrounding landscape, while the vineyards added a working agricultural element to the luxury estate.Why Robin Williams listed the estate for $35 millionWilliams first put Villa Sorriso on the market in 2012 with an asking price of $35 million. Contemporary reports said he had spoken publicly about financial pressures associated with his divorces and explained that he needed to sell the property. When the original listing failed to attract a buyer, the estate was removed from the market before returning in 2014 at a reduced price of $29.9 million. After Williams died in August 2014, the property remained on the market and was subsequently offered at lower prices. By the time it sold, the asking price had fallen to $22.9 million. The long marketing period shows how difficult it was to find a buyer willing to purchase such a large and highly specialised property.How the $35 million asking price became an $18.1 million saleThe eventual sale represented a substantial reduction from the property's original asking price. The Los Angeles Times reported that Villa Sorriso sold for $18.1 million in cash in January 2016, four years after it was first listed. The final price was roughly 48% below the original $35 million asking price. By then, the property had passed through several asking prices, including $29.9 million, $25.9 million and finally $22.9 million. The sale was reported as an all-cash transaction, with Joyce Rey and Cyd Greer of Coldwell Banker representing the listing. The buyers were French winemakers Alfred and Melanie Tesseron, who were interested in the estate's vineyard potential.What happened to Robin Williams' Napa estate after the saleThe sale gave Villa Sorriso a new chapter beyond its connection with Williams. Alfred and Melanie Tesseron, owners of Château Pontet-Canet in Bordeaux, acquired the property as their first California wine estate. The estate contained vineyards planted with varieties including Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot, and the new owners planned to develop its winemaking potential. The property has since remained connected to Napa's wine industry while retaining its association with Williams. Its story therefore extends beyond the celebrity real-estate market. What began as Williams' secluded mountain retreat became a vineyard estate under new ownership, while the enormous mansion, surrounding landscape and decades-long Hollywood connection continued to make Villa Sorriso one of Napa Valley's more unusual properties.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘The moment US left, attacks resumed’: Russia launches fresh assault on Ukraine, 3 killed
articles.summary: Europe News: Russia launched a fresh wave of drone and missile attacks on Kyiv early Tuesday, killing three people and wounding 16 others, as fires broke out acros.
articles.body: Russia launched a fresh wave of drone and missile attacks on Kyiv early Tuesday, killing three people and wounding 16 others, as fires broke out across the Ukrainian capital.The strikes came after a brief pause during a visit by US peace negotiators. Interior minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said 16 people were wounded in the city.“Kyiv was exploding and burning,” EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarina Mathernova said.The attack damaged at least 14 high-rise buildings, as well as a dormitory, school, clinic, warehouses and other sites, officials were quoted as saying by Reuters.Russia resumed its attacks after US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff left Kyiv on Sunday following talks with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as the Trump administration renewed efforts to end Russia’s 4 and a half year war in Ukraine.The envoys had arrived in Kyiv after talks in Moscow, following which the Kremlin said it did not rule out the resumption of three-way negotiations."The moment the US president's peace envoys left, (Russian President Vladimir) Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X.Both Moscow and Kyiv halted strikes on their respective capitals for three days to ensure the safety of the US peace negotiators. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha urged allies to increase pressure on Moscow and provide interceptors to counter ballistic missiles, saying Kyiv’s stocks had fallen to critically low levels.Before the talks, Russia had intensified air attacks on Kyiv and surrounding areas, with strikes occurring almost around the clock rather than mainly at night. The attacks involved faster, jet-propelled drones that killed residents and disrupted daily activities.The Russian defence ministry said Moscow had struck military and logistics targets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, as well as in the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, Russian news agencies reported.Aside from Kyiv, eight other regions were targeted in the attacks, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said. articles.title: Man accused of Great Denham triple murder admits gun charges
articles.summary: A man is in court in South Africa two months after his wife and daughters are found dead in the UK.
articles.body:
A man accused of killing his wife and two daughters in the UK has admitted unlawful possession of a firearm and ammunition in South Africa.

Nothabo Zandile Tshuma, 42, and her daughters Natalie, 15, and Nala, five, were found with fatal head injuries in Great Denham, near Bedford, on 7 July.

Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma, 45, was arrested in Johannesburg after leaving the UK. South African police said he was found with a gun and ammunition he bought in the country and he has appeared before magistrates in the city for a plea hearing.

The Crown Prosecution Service in England has authorised three murder charges against Tshuma and an extradition hearing is due to take place in South Africa on Thursday.

The defendant is a British citizen of Zimbabwean heritage.

He could face sentencing for the gun offences later.

articles.title: O2 Academy Sheffield set for 2027 reopen after refurbishment
articles.summary: The venue closed in September 2023 due to concerns about its unstable roof.
articles.body:
The O2 Academy Sheffield is set to reopen in February 2027 following a four-year closure for major refurbishment work.

The music venue, which temporarily closed in September 2023, will have a new roof, air conditioning and a state-of-the-art sound system, organisers said.

Originally opened in 1968 as the Top Rank Suite, the Arundel Gate site has hosted gigs by artists including The Police, The Clash, Joy Division and David Bowie over the last forty years.

A spokesperson for Academy Music Group (AMG), the venue's owners, said: "Having welcomed legendary artists to the stage, it has a brilliant musical heritage that we're helping to carry forward."

The venue closed due to areas of unstable reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (Raac), a lightweight material prone to collapse, in the roof.

The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) warned that Raac, which was used extensively in the 1950s and 60s, was beyond its lifespan and could "collapse with little or no notice".

Sheffield City Council granted permission in February for the problematic roof deck to be replaced with the new flat one.

Commenting on the venue's opening date, Liam Boylan, chief executive officer of AMG said the Sheffield site was an "important venue in the region".

"One that promoters and artists will have missed being able to include on their routing whilst it has been closed."

The venue was acquired by AMG in 2008 and other notable acts to play there include The Prodigy, Kasabian, Self Esteem, The Streets, The Killers and Stormzy.

articles.title: The American couple who restored ‘The African Queen’ have now bought a Scottish castle for £3.9 million
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A Scottish castle once shaped by a family dispute is about to begin another chapter, this time under the ownership of an American couple with a histor.
articles.body: A Scottish castle once shaped by a family dispute is about to begin another chapter, this time under the ownership of an American couple with a history of bringing old attractions back to life. According to the Scottish Licensed Trade News, Suzanne and Lance Holmquist have bought Carbisdale Castle in Sutherland for just under £3.9 million, with plans to turn parts of the Grade A-listed property into a boutique hotel. For Suzanne, the purchase also has a personal connection. She grew up in Glasgow before moving to the United States, where she and Lance built a tourism business in the Florida Keys. The couple are already familiar with ambitious restoration work. They previously helped revive The African Queen, the 1912 steam launch made famous by Humphrey Bogart and Katharine Hepburn. Now their attention has shifted from a historic boat to a Highland castle, with short-term stays planned first and a larger hotel intended to follow.How a Florida couple ended up buying a Scottish castleSuzanne Holmquist left Scotland for the United States after beginning her career as a television editor. She eventually settled in the Florida Keys, where she and her husband built a tourism business around the water.According to The Press and Journal, Lance had arrived in Key Largo in 1988, after years spent surfing and working in diving businesses, including time around Australia's Great Barrier Reef. The couple have been married for two decades and have three children. Their business, Calypso Sailing, operates sailing trips, catamaran charters and private cruises around Key Largo and Key West.Scotland, however, never disappeared from Suzanne’s life. She continued travelling back and forth and retained an interest in the country’s historic buildings. The search for Carbisdale began after a different castle caught her attention, only for her to discover that it had already been sold.That disappointment appears to have turned into a much longer search. Suzanne eventually found Carbisdale, a property with enough space and history to fit what she had been looking for. She and Lance spent months working towards the purchase, alongside a 10% partner, before completing the deal.Their immediate focus is not a full restoration of the building. They want to get guests through the doors first.The restoration project that prepared them for CarbisdaleThe castle is not the first ambitious restoration project the Holmquists have taken on. Their earlier project was considerably smaller in scale, but it carried a name recognised far beyond the Florida Keys.The couple took on the restoration of The African Queen, the 1912 steam launch used by Humphrey Bogart and Katharine Hepburn in the 1951 film of the same name.The vessel had originally been built in England as the S/L Livingstone. Before becoming a piece of cinema history, it was used in East Africa to carry missionaries, goods and hunting parties along inland waterways.After its film career, the boat continued changing hands and eventually deteriorated. Reportedly, in 2012, the Holmquists entered into a long-term lease and began bringing it back into working condition.The restoration involved replacing parts of the hull and installing a new boiler, while retaining the character associated with the vessel seen on screen. Once the work was completed, The African Queen returned to service in Key Largo, where it is now used for cruises and private charters.The couple also became involved in the Humphrey Bogart Film Festival, extending their interest in the film beyond the boat itself.Carbisdale is a considerably different proposition. This time, they have a large historic building rather than a 1912 launch to bring back into active use.The ‘Castle of Spite’ has changed roles many timesCarbisdale Castle was constructed in the early 20th century for the Dowager Duchess of Sutherland. Building work took place between 1905 and 1917, although sources give slightly different dates within that period, as reported by The Scottish Licensed Trade News.Its unusual local nickname, the ‘Castle of Spite’, comes from the family tensions surrounding its construction. The building was intended as a home for the Duchess following a dispute within the Sutherland family, giving the castle a backstory that is almost as well known locally as its architecture.The property was used as a private residence before becoming associated with the Second World War and later spending more than 60 years as a youth hostel. It eventually returned to private ownership.Lady Carbisdale, its previous owner, carried out substantial restoration work and spent millions of pounds on the property. Her decision to sell came with the recognition that the next stage would require someone prepared to take the building into a more commercial future.The couple’s plans go beyond rooms to create a Scottish experienceThe couple's plan is to move gradually rather than attempt to complete every part of the property at once.Their first target is short-term accommodation for up to 19 guests. They hope to have that operating within a month of the purchase. Within roughly a year, the intention is to have a boutique hotel with as many as 14 rooms.There is more space available beyond that initial phase. A further 20 rooms in an unrenovated wing have been identified for possible future development, although those plans are further down the line.Suzanne has spoken of creating a high-tea operation inside the castle, using an upstairs dining room as a tribute to the Duchess who commissioned the building. She is also considering a house whisky, with ‘Skull Scotch’ among the names being explored, a reference to Lance’s seafaring background.“There’s an upstairs dining room which I’m going to create as a homage to the Duchess who built this castle.”The Holmquists are turning Carbisdale into a family affairThe Holmquists are treating Carbisdale as a family business rather than a project that will sit separately from their lives in Florida.Their two daughters are at university in Florida and are expected to contribute to marketing and social media. Their 11-year-old son will attend a local school in Scotland.Lance is also expected to keep running the couple’s boating business in Florida, although they are reducing its scale as the family takes on the castle. That arrangement leaves the couple with businesses on opposite sides of the Atlantic, at least for the time being.Suzanne has also made clear that the family wants to establish links with people living around Carbisdale rather than operate as an isolated private venture. Jobs created through the hotel are expected to form part of the local economic contribution, while the property itself will become more accessible to visitors.A new commercial future is taking shape at Carbisdale CastleThe purchase gives Carbisdale Castle a commercial future after years in which its use has shifted from family home to wartime refuge, hostel and private estate.The Holmquists are bringing experience from a very different tourism market, but the African Queen restoration gives some indication of how they approach historic properties. Their Florida business has also given them experience in hospitality and attracting visitors.The castle will require considerably more work before the full hotel vision is realised. For the moment, the first stage is straightforward: prepare part of the building for guests, begin operating short-term stays and work towards the larger hotel.Suzanne’s connection to Scotland adds another dimension to the purchase. She left Glasgow years ago, but the decision to buy a Highland castle means that part of her working life has now come back to the country where it began.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
